source.title: SemanticCamo: Jailbreaking Large Language Models through Semantic Camouflage
source.authors: Ji-Hui Yan; Xiaocui Yang; Da-Ling Wang; Shi Feng; Yi-Fei Zhang; Yinzhi Zhao

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates harmful-response rates under a different intervention—a semantic-camouflage jailbreak—but does not test the claim's specified fine-tuning or first-token mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-response rates for SemanticCamo and its defenses, but its intervention is semantic camouflage, not fine-tuning, token-prefilling, suffixes, or decoding changes. It reports no aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or weight localization test. Rows use versions ["none"] because the results do not measure a listed version. Baseline attack methods in Table 1 are not catalogued as rows because they are comparisons between attack methods, not tests of the claim's interventions. The helpfulness evaluations and feature-construction/inference measures do not measure a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a black-box jailbreak, SemanticCamo, that rewrites harmful queries into semantic-feature prompts. It involves no fine-tuning, no per-token KL, no prefilling, suffix or decoding intervention, no weight localization and no deepening training, so its results bear on no version. It cites Qi et al. 2024 only for the GPT-4o judge and harmfulness score. The reader's 'tests/T2' is wrong: a different jailbreak family is not a test of any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that safety alignment generalizes poorly when harmful semantics are replaced with semantic features. They find SemanticCamo averages over 80% ASR and that the tested defenses are largely ineffective.
record.recipe_differences: A black-box prompt-based semantic-camouflage jailbreak, not fine-tuning or an intervention on the response's opening tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported ASR changes with the defense applied; the text also says the number and choice of semantic features affect attack performance.

fits_no_version.finding: SemanticCamo reaches ASR of 66.73–89.81% across six models on AdvBench, and several input defenses reduce it only modestly or not at all.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic-camouflage prompts elicit harmful responses from multiple aligned LLMs, and common input defenses leave substantial ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: SemanticCamo responses receive GPT-4o-judged harmfulness scores of 3.94–4.84 out of 5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Responses elicited by semantic camouflage are judged highly harmful.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of ACL 2025)
record.problems: The study evaluates a particular semantic-camouflage attack rather than the fine-tuning or token-position mechanisms in the claim. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the ASR results. Several attack results and ablations are presented in figures without fully tabulated numeric values.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 6 reports ASR by number of semantic features but does not provide tabulated values; Figure 4 reports ASR by iteration but does not clearly identify the evaluated target model in the text. Other semantic-method comparisons in Table 7 and helpfulness, faithfulness, feature-construction, and inference results were omitted because they do not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance; not studied.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance; not studied.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models by response position; not measured.
Prefilling a compliant opening, adversarial suffixes and decoding changes are not studied as the paper's intervention. GCG appears only as a transferred baseline.
Localization of safety in weights or ranks; not tested. GradSafe is used only as an input-detection defense.
The causes of shallowness in data or objective; not tested. The paper only argues from competing objectives and mismatched generalization.
Training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens; not tested.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Their 'observed' states refer to the attack's own effect, not to any version. Table 1 also reports the authors' run of GCG as a transferred suffix baseline: 89.6% ASR on GPT-3.5, 0% on GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude and Llama-3-70B, and 43.07% on DeepSeek-v3. This is a baseline comparison of transferred suffixes on black-box APIs, not a test of V4's opening-token mechanism, so it is not added as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning, its data quantity, and refusal/compliance after fine-tuning.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models and its distribution across response positions.
Compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes; SemanticCamo is a different attack intervention and does not measure bypass via the first response tokens.
Localization of safety behaviour in weights, parameters, or ranks.
Whether data or the training objective causes safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety across response tokens and whether that change is robust.
